hints.title: Comparing Friends Songs
hints.text: Join listens with friendship such that user1 and user2 are already friends, then compare their song lists on the same day.

hints.title: Aggregating Same Day Listens
hints.text: Group by user1_id, user2_id, and day, counting the distinct song_ids heard by both users.

hints.title: Meeting the Three Song Threshold
hints.text: Use a having clause requiring count(distinct song_id) >= 3, and return unique user1_id and user2_id pairs.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT DISTINCT
    f.user1_id,
    f.user2_id
FROM Friendship f
JOIN Listens l1
    ON f.user1_id = l1.user_id
JOIN Listens l2
    ON f.user2_id = l2.user_id
    AND l1.day = l2.day
    AND l1.song_id = l2.song_id
GROUP BY f.user1_id, f.user2_id, l1.day
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT l1.song_id) >= 3;
```

complexity.time: O(F * S) where F is friends and S is average listens per user
complexity.space: O(F) space for distinct friend pairs
variables: S: average number of listens per user
complexity.notes: Joining friends with identical daily songs and filtering via HAVING.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Omitting distinct song counting can miscount duplicate plays of the same track.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Joining directly through the Friendship table restricts candidates early.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Candidate should maintain the canonical user1_id < user2_id ordering from Friendship.

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def leetcodify_similar_friends(listens: pd.DataFrame, friendship: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    m = pd.merge(friendship, listens, left_on='user1_id', right_on='user_id')
    m = pd.merge(m, listens, left_on=['user2_id', 'day', 'song_id'], right_on=['user_id', 'day', 'song_id'])
    g = m.groupby(['user1_id', 'user2_id', 'day'])['song_id'].nunique().reset_index()
    res = g[g['song_id'] >= 3][['user1_id', 'user2_id']].drop_duplicates()
    return res
